topic: how applications are read (reading models and time per file)
speaker_role: former admissions officer who read for three institutions (about 12 years at one liberal arts college), interviewed by the channel host
commercial_incentive: Host runs a college-advice channel and podcast; no direct sales pitch in this segment.
key_insights: The time per file depends on which read is being described: first reader, territory manager or committee; quoted minutes are meaningless without that context.
In one common model the first reader is the only person who reads every word, and later readers rely on that reader's ratings and summary.
Colleges use several models: solo first reader with a recommendation, a preparer feeding a territory manager, and two-person committee-based evaluation with heavy up-front time.
Few schools send every applicant to committee; some allow one reader to deny (with a dean sign-off) but not to admit.
Selective colleges front-load a thorough read, then later committees move quickly through summary evaluations.
A non-competitive academic profile can put a file into fast skim mode, whereas files from under-resourced backgrounds at colleges with composition goals get a slower read.
Experienced readers can extract in minutes what novices need much longer for; one reads the essay's first and last paragraphs to gauge how much time to give it.
Less selective colleges may make a single pass, sometimes with automated screening of self-reported academics.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Susan (guest): first-reader time of 15 to 30 minutes at her liberal arts college, with a 1-to-7 rating scale; hardly anyone was admitted below an academic 3 without a hook.
Susan: preparer role goal of no more than 15 minutes; committee-based evaluation involves two people for about 15 to 20 minutes each.
Susan and Mark: current first-read times of about 5 to 20 minutes, with 5 more common than 20.
Mark: UCLA reportedly pays seasonal readers about $2.57 per read (over 250 readers; $2,575 per 1,000 reads) and receives over 50,000 applications.
Mark: Davidson reads every early decision file in committee; Duke uses a one-reader deny model with dean sign-off.
notable_or_distinctive: Clarifies why 'minutes per file' figures conflict by separating reading models, with a specific reader-pay figure for UCLA.
reliability_notes: Facts about specific schools (UCLA pay, Duke, Davidson) are stated by the host from memory and may be dated; the guest's last name is not given and captions have some garbling.
